slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Soil is the most mysterious and most central element of terroir. In Bordeaux, gravel, clay, limestone, sand, and silt form a unique soil mosaic, with each soil type telling a different wine story. The gravel of the Left Bank imparts robust structure to Cabernet Sauvignon, while the clay of the Right Bank allows Merlot to express its supple texture.

This course takes you deep underground — from geological origins to the principles of soil science, from physical and chemical properties to biological activity — for a comprehensive understanding of how soil influences vine growth and shapes wine style. We will explore the secrets of Bordeaux's five major soil types and reveal why the gravel of Château Latour and the blue clay of Château Pétrus can produce world-class wines.

Course Learning Objectives

🔬 Master the Core Concepts of Soil Science

Understand key indicators such as soil texture, structure, pH, and drainage, and build a professional soil analysis framework

🗺️ In-depth Understanding of Bordeaux's 5 Major Soil Types

Learn about the geological origins, distribution areas, and unique characteristics of gravel, clay, limestone, sand, and silt

🍇 Analyse the Mechanism by Which Soil Affects Grapes

Understand how soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties affect root development, water and nutrient supply, and fruit quality

🍷 Learn to Infer Wine Style from Soil Characteristics

Master the connections between different soil types and wine structure, tannin, acidity, and aromatic style

🌍 Explore the Science and Philosophy of Terroir

Understand the scientific basis of the terroir concept and the new challenges for soil management under climate change

On completing this course, you will be able to deeply interpret Bordeaux wines from a soil perspective, understanding why each plot of land can give rise to a unique terroir expression.

Estimated study time: 45 minutes

Difficulty level: Advanced Professional
slides.1.title: Foundation Framework of Soil Science
slides.1.subtitle: Understanding the Three Dimensions of Soil
slides.2.title: Core Soil Properties: Three Dimensions
slides.2.content:
⚙️
Physical Properties
Physical Properties
Determines water and air movement, providing the basic environment for root growth.
  • Texture: sand/silt/clay ratio → drainage/water retention
  • Structure: degree of aggregate formation → root penetration/aeration
  • Depth: explorable root layer range
  • Drainage: too fast or too slow both affect quality
  • Thermal capacity: ability to store and release heat
Most intuitive; directly affects vine vigour and ripening pace
⚗️
Chemical Properties
Chemical Properties
Determines available nutrients and how they are accessed, affecting vine health and quality.
  • pH: nutrient availability (ideal 6.5–7.5)
  • Minerals: impact of Ca/Mg/K/Fe on quality
  • Organic matter: fertility and microbial activity
  • CEC: nutrient-holding capacity
  • NPK balance: growth and fruit quality
Controls nutritional status and overall vine health
🦠
Biological Properties
Biological Properties
Soil is a living ecosystem; microbial activity is key to health and resilience.
  • Microbial diversity: bacteria/fungi/actinomycetes
  • Mycorrhizae: symbiotic with roots, aiding water and nutrient uptake
  • Soil respiration: indicator of microbial activity
  • Organic matter decomposition: core of the nutrient cycle
  • Disease/pest suppression: self-protection of healthy soil
The foundation of soil health and long-term sustainability
slides.3.title: Three-Level Framework for Soil Analysis
slides.3.content:
Understanding soil from macro to micro
🌋 Geological Level
Millions of years
Geological Level
🔍 Research Focus
Parent rock type, geological history, depositional processes
📌 Example
Günz glacial period Garonne river deposits forming Médoc gravel
🛠 Geological maps · Borehole sampling · Geophysical surveys
🌱 Pedological Level
Thousands to tens of thousands of years
Pedological Level
🔍 Research Focus
Soil profile, horizon structure, degree of development
📌 Example
Pomerol's iron-rich clay layer (crasse de fer)
🛠 Soil profile analysis · Physical/chemical tests · Microscopy
🌿 Rhizosphere Level
Seasonal variation
Rhizosphere Level
🔍 Research Focus
Root–soil–microorganism interactions
📌 Example
Vine root exudates and mycorrhizal fungal symbiosis
🛠 Root observation · Microbial sequencing · Soil respiration measurement
💡 Understanding soil requires spanning multiple timescales — from geological evolution (millions of years) to current biological interactions (the current season)
slides.4.title: Knowledge Check: Soil Basics
slides.4.question: In viticulture, which soil property most directly influences root depth and water access?
slides.4.options.0: The chemical pH of the soil
slides.4.options.1: The physical texture and structure of the soil
slides.4.options.2: The organic matter content of the soil
slides.4.options.3: The microbial diversity of the soil
slides.4.explanation: The physical properties of soil — especially texture (sand, silt, clay ratio) and structure (how particles aggregate) — directly determine the depth roots can penetrate, as well as drainage and water-retention capacity. This is the basic environment for root growth. Chemical and biological properties are important but depend on a suitable physical structure.
slides.5.title: Bordeaux's Soil Mosaic
slides.5.subtitle: Five Major Soil Types and Geographic Distribution
slides.6.title: The Geological History of Bordeaux's Soil Formation
slides.7.title: Soil Type ① Gravel Soil (Gravel / Graves) 🪨
slides.7.content:
🪨 Gravel Soil (Gravel / Graves)

French: Graves

📍 Geographic Distribution

Left Bank Médoc, Graves appellation

🌍 Geological Origin

Quaternary glacial river deposits, mainly from the Pyrenees

🔬 Soil Composition

  • Main components: Quartz and granite gravel (2–20 cm diameter)
  • Secondary components: Coarse sand, small amounts of clay
  • Depth: 1–4 m gravel layer, with clay or sandy clay beneath

⚗️ Physical Properties

  • Drainage: Excellent — porous structure, rapid water infiltration
  • Water retention: Low — deep root system required
  • Thermal capacity: High — absorbs heat by day, releases it at night, extending the ripening period
  • Reflectivity: High — reflects sunlight, increasing photosynthesis

🧪 Chemical Properties

  • pH: 6.5–7.0 (slightly acidic to neutral)
  • Fertility: Low to medium — low fertility promotes quality
  • Minerals: Moderate levels of iron and potassium

🍇 Most Suitable Grape Variety

Cabernet Sauvignon (late-ripening, requires ample heat)

  • Excellent drainage prevents root rot
  • Heat storage promotes slow, even ripening
  • Moderate water stress concentrates flavours
  • Low fertility controls yields

🍷 Wine Style Characteristics

  • Strong structure: rich, firm tannins
  • Long ageing potential: 15–30 years or more
  • Minerality: graphite, pencil shavings character
  • Dark fruit dominant: blackcurrant, black cherry
  • Elegant restraint: rather than overripeness

🏆 Top Representative Châteaux

Château Latour, Château Margaux, Château Haut-Brion

🌡️ Climate Adaptability

Requires irrigation management in dry years; drainage advantage is more pronounced in wet years
slides.8.title: Soil Type ② Clay (Clay / Argile) 🧱
slides.8.content:
🧱 Clay (Clay / Argile)

French: Argile

📍 Geographic Distribution

Right Bank Pomerol, Saint-Émilion plain

🌍 Geological Origin

Ancient marine sediments, river alluvial deposits

🔬 Soil Composition

  • Main components: Clay minerals (smectite, illite)
  • Secondary components: Silt, small amounts of sand
  • Depth: Deep, can reach several metres

⚗️ Physical Properties

  • Drainage: Poor to moderate — fine particles, slow drainage
  • Water retention: Very high — absorbs water in wet season, releases it in drought
  • Thermal capacity: Medium — warms slowly, retains heat well
  • Workability: Heavy and sticky when wet, hard when dry

🧪 Chemical Properties

  • pH: 7.0–8.0 (neutral to slightly alkaline)
  • Fertility: High — rich in minerals
  • CEC: High — strong nutrient-holding capacity
  • Minerals: Rich in iron, magnesium, potassium (Pomerol's iron-rich clay is especially renowned)

🍇 Most Suitable Grape Variety

Merlot (early-ripening, suited to water-retentive environments)

  • Water retention is an advantage during drought
  • Rich nutrients support Merlot's early growth
  • Clay's cooling effect prevents overripeness
  • Minerals impart complexity

🍷 Wine Style Characteristics

  • Full body: plump, rounded texture
  • Soft tannins: velvety mouthfeel
  • Deep fruit: plum, blackberry, cherry
  • Mineral complexity: earth, truffle, iron ore
  • Earlier drinking window: 5–15 years

⭐ Special Type: Crasse de fer (Iron Pan)

Pomerol's unique iron-enriched hardpan layer, rich in iron oxides, imparts minerality and distinctive aromas

Located 30–80 cm below the surface

🏆 Top Representative Châteaux

Pétrus, Château Le Pin, Château Lafleur

🌡️ Climate Adaptability

Drainage pressure increases in wet years; a distinct advantage in drought years
slides.9.title: Soil Type ③ Limestone (Limestone / Calcaire) ⛰️
slides.9.content:
⛰️ Limestone (Limestone / Calcaire)

French: Calcaire

📍 Geographic Distribution

Saint-Émilion plateau, Côtes appellations

🌍 Geological Origin

Deposits of ancient marine organism skeletons (Tertiary period, approximately 30–60 million years ago)

🔬 Soil Composition

  • Main components: High calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) content
  • Secondary components: Mixed clay and silt
  • Depth: Bedrock type or weathered layer, variable depth

⚗️ Physical Properties

  • Drainage: Good — highly porous
  • Water retention: Moderate — internal water storage
  • Thermal capacity: High — white colour reflects light, but good heat retention
  • Root penetration: Good — roots can penetrate easily through fissures

🧪 Chemical Properties

  • pH: 7.5–8.5 (alkaline)
  • Calcium content: Very high — influences tannin structure
  • Fertility: Moderate — requires organic matter supplementation
  • Mineral composition: Calcium and magnesium dominant

🍇 Most Suitable Grape Varieties

Cabernet Franc, Merlot

  • High calcium content forms refined tannins
  • Excellent drainage maintains freshness
  • Strong minerality highlights terroir character
  • Cooling effect preserves acidity

🍷 Wine Style Characteristics

  • Elegant and refined: light but not lacking depth
  • Strong minerality: chalk, wet stone, saline note
  • Lively acidity: fresh and bright
  • Refined tannins: silky and smooth
  • Prominent floral notes: violet, rose

📊 Limestone Sub-types

  • Hard limestone (calcaire à astéries): Top of the Saint-Émilion plateau, best drainage
  • Soft limestone (molasse): More highly weathered, higher clay content

🏆 Top Representative Châteaux

Château Ausone, Château Pavie, Château Canon

🌡️ Climate Adaptability

Good drought resistance, but thin topsoil requires irrigation in extreme drought
slides.10.title: Soil Type ④ Sand (Sand / Sable) 🏖️
slides.10.content:
🏖️ Sand (Sand / Sable)

French: Sable

📍 Geographic Distribution

Coastal areas of Médoc, parts of Entre-Deux-Mers

🌍 Geological Origin

Ancient riverbeds, aeolian deposits

🔬 Soil Composition

  • Main components: Quartz sand (0.05–2 mm diameter)
  • Secondary components: Small amounts of clay and organic matter
  • Depth: Deep, several metres

⚗️ Physical Properties

  • Drainage: Very fast — large inter-particle gaps
  • Water retention: Very low — high drought risk
  • Thermal capacity: Low — heats and cools rapidly
  • Workability: Easy to cultivate

🧪 Chemical Properties

  • pH: 6.0–7.0 (slightly acidic to neutral)
  • Fertility: Low — poor
  • CEC: Low — difficult to retain nutrients
  • Organic matter: Low

🍇 Most Suitable Grape Varieties

Early-ripening varieties (Merlot), post-phylloxera replanting

  • Phylloxera cannot survive in sandy soil
  • Drainage prevents root disease
  • Low yields concentrate flavours
  • Early-ripening characteristics

🍷 Wine Style Characteristics

  • Light and delicate: relatively light body
  • Fruit-forward: dominated by red fruits
  • Soft tannins: lacking structural backbone
  • Earlier drinking window: 3–8 years
  • Aromatic: notable floral and fruit aromas

⚠️ Management Challenges

  • Severe drought stress
  • Insufficient fertility requires management
  • Limited ageing potential
  • Lower market recognition

🌡️ Opportunity under Climate Change

Warming may enhance the value of sandy soil appellations (drainage and early-ripening advantages)
slides.11.title: Soil Type ⑤ Clay-Limestone Mix (Clay-Limestone) 🌋
slides.11.content:
🌋 Clay-Limestone Mix (Clay-Limestone)

French: Argilo-calcaire

📍 Geographic Distribution

Saint-Émilion Côtes, Fronsac

🌍 Geological Origin

Limestone weathering mixed with clay deposits

🔬 Soil Composition

  • Main components: Mixture of clay and calcium carbonate
  • Secondary components: Rich in minerals
  • Ratio: Clay : limestone = 40–60% : 30–50%

⚗️ Physical Properties

  • Drainage: Good to moderate
  • Water retention: Medium to high
  • Thermal capacity: Moderate
  • Versatility: High — combines drainage and water retention

🧪 Chemical Properties

  • pH: 7.0–8.0 (neutral to slightly alkaline)
  • Fertility: Medium to high
  • Mineral complexity: Balanced calcium, iron, magnesium

🍇 Most Suitable Grape Varieties

Merlot, Cabernet Franc blend

  • Balanced water management
  • Clay provides fullness, limestone provides freshness
  • High mineral complexity
  • Strong adaptability

🍷 Wine Style Characteristics

  • Well-balanced: combines clay's richness and limestone's elegance
  • High complexity: multi-layered flavours
  • Ageing potential: 10–20 years
  • Mineral and fruit character in equal measure

⭐ Unique Advantage

Regarded as the "most perfectly balanced" soil, combining the best of both soil types

🏆 Top Representative Châteaux

Château Angélus, Château Cheval Blanc (some parcels)

slides.13.title: Knowledge Check: Soil Types
slides.13.question: What is the key soil characteristic that allows Château Pétrus to produce one of the world's finest Merlot wines?
slides.13.options.0: Deep gravel layers providing excellent drainage
slides.13.options.1: A unique iron-rich clay layer (crasse de fer)
slides.13.explanation: Château Pétrus lies at the heart of the Pomerol appellation. Its vineyard has a unique 'crasse de fer' (iron pan) — a hardened clay layer rich in iron oxides. This soil has extremely high water retention, providing stable moisture for Merlot in drought years; it is also rich in minerals, giving the wine deep, concentrated fruit, a velvety texture, and unique mineral complexity. The high iron content also imparts the characteristic aromas of truffle and earth.
slides.14.title: The Transformation Mechanism from Soil to Wine Glass
slides.14.subtitle: Scientifically Decoding Terroir
slides.15.title: Soil→Grape Pathway ① Water Stress and Concentration
slides.15.content:
🔬 Mechanism

Drainage and water retention determine vine water status. Moderate water stress promotes quality.

📊 Specific Effects

Mild stress → growth redirected to fruit; skin-to-pulp ratio increases; berries become smaller; roots extend deeper

⚖️ Soil Comparison

Gravel: Greater stress → higher concentration

Clay: Less stress → fuller body

The key is avoiding excessive or insufficient water stress
slides.16.title: Soil→Grape Pathway ② Mineral Uptake and Flavour
slides.16.content:
🧪 Mechanism and Key Points

Mineral elements are taken up through the root system and participate in metabolic processes, influencing the synthesis of aroma and flavour compounds.

⚗️ Functions of Key Mineral Elements

  • Ca (calcium): Cell wall structure and tannin refinement
  • Fe (iron): Colour depth and mineral aromas
  • Mg (magnesium): Chlorophyll synthesis and sugar accumulation
  • K (potassium): Water and sugar transport
  • N (nitrogen): Generation of aroma precursors (in moderate amounts)

💡 Scientific Perspective

The precise source of 'minerality' in wine remains debated in academia, but mineral composition clearly has a profound influence on vine physiology and the synthesis of flavour compounds.
slides.17.title: Soil→Grape Pathway ③ Root Depth and Complexity
slides.17.content:
🌱 Depth Stratification Effects

  • Shallow roots (0–50 cm): Greatly affected by climate and water fluctuations
  • Mid-level (50–150 cm): More stable nutrient and water supply
  • Deep roots (150–300 cm+): Rich in minerals, strong drought resistance, increased complexity

🪨 Root Performance in Different Soils

  • Limestone: Fissure structure promotes deep root development
  • Clay: High penetration resistance but wide nutrient distribution
  • Gravel: Medium depth, stable root development

🎯 The Secret of Complexity

Multi-layered soil structures (e.g., gravel topsoil over clay subsoil) often produce more complex flavour expression, as roots can absorb diverse nutrients and minerals from different depths.
slides.18.title: Soil→Grape Pathway ④ Microbiome and Health
slides.18.content:
🦠 Key Roles

Soil microbial communities influence nutrient transformation, disease suppression, and root health, indirectly affecting grape quality.

🔬 Main Microbial Types and Functions

  • Mycorrhizal fungi: Expand root uptake surface area
  • Nitrogen-fixing bacteria: Supply available nitrogen
  • Antagonistic bacteria: Suppress pathogens, reduce disease
  • Decomposers: Break down organic matter, release nutrients

🌿 Management Methods

Organic farming and biodynamic practices (Biodynamic) can significantly enhance soil microbial diversity and activity.

🔍 Frontier Perspective

The soil microbiome may be a 'hidden dimension' of terroir — differences in microbial communities between soils may explain part of a terroir's uniqueness.
slides.19.title: Soil→Grape Pathway ⑤ Temperature Regulation and Ripening
slides.19.content:
🌡️ Thermal Effects

The thermal capacity and colour of soil influence its temperature profile, which in turn alters the ripening pace and final style of grapes.

🎨 Thermal Characteristics of Different Soils

  • White gravel/limestone: Reflects sunlight, accelerates ripening
  • Dark clay: Releases heat slowly at night, extending the ripening period
  • Sand: Temperature rises and falls rapidly, helping to preserve acidity
  • Deep gravel: Stores heat, providing additional thermal energy

⏰ Example: The Gravel Advantage in Médoc

The deep gravel of the Médoc can provide an additional 2–3 weeks of effective heat accumulation for the late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon — one of the key advantages that allows this appellation to achieve perfect Cabernet Sauvignon ripeness.
slides.20.title: 🎯 Soil–Variety–Style Relationship Matrix
slides.20.content:
Analysing wine style expression through soil characteristics, and understanding the scientific basis of terroir

💡 Important Note

Soil is the cornerstone of terroir, but a wine's final style is jointly determined by five major factors: soil × variety selection × vintage climate × winemaking technique × estate philosophy. The matrix above shows the typical expression for each soil type; actual results will vary with specific parcel microclimate and winemaker style.
slides.21.title: Case Study: The Soil Miracle of Château Cheval Blanc
slides.21.soilComposition.description: The vineyard is divided into 45 parcels, each with different soil composition
slides.21.quote.text: We are not making a single wine — we are orchestrating 45 different voices to create a symphony.
slides.21.quote.title: General Manager, Château Cheval Blanc
slides.22.title: Knowledge Check: Soil Mechanisms
slides.22.question: Why is the deep gravel soil of Médoc especially suited to late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon?
slides.22.options.0: Gravel provides abundant nutrients to promote rapid ripening
slides.22.options.1: The high thermal capacity of gravel releases heat at night, extending the effective ripening period
slides.22.options.2: Gravel soil's high water retention ensures sufficient moisture
slides.22.options.3: Gravel's white colour reflects cool light, lowering grape temperature
slides.22.explanation: The deep gravel layer of the Médoc (up to 3–4 m) has high thermal mass. During the day, the gravel absorbs large amounts of solar radiation; at night and on overcast days, it slowly releases this heat, providing grapes with an additional warm environment. This effectively extends the ripening period for late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon by 2–3 weeks, allowing it to achieve perfect ripeness in Bordeaux's relatively cool oceanic climate. This is the key soil advantage that makes Médoc a home for Cabernet Sauvignon.
slides.23.title: Soil Management and Practice
slides.23.subtitle: Integrated Management from Surface to Rhizosphere
slides.24.title: Surface Management: Cover Crops and Weed Suppression
slides.24.content:
🌿
Cover Crops
Actively improving soil structure
Increase soil organic matter, improve aggregate structure, promote microbial activity, and can fix nitrogen or suppress weeds.
🌾 Common Combinations
  • Grasses — increase organic matter
  • Legumes — fix nitrogen
  • Composites — biological biopore loosening
✅ Reduce erosion · Improve water holding · Stabilise temperature · Improve trafficability
🪵
Mulch
Reduce evaporation · suppress weeds · protect topsoil
Wood chips, straw, or grape pomace mulch can reduce evaporation, suppress weeds, and protect the topsoil life layer.
⚠️ Management Notes
  • Manage rodent populations
  • Watch for nitrogen lock-up risk
  • Adjust thickness flexibly by vintage
✅ Significantly reduces irrigation needs in dry years
slides.25.title: Water Management and Soil Structure Maintenance
slides.25.content:
💧
Precision Irrigation
Where regulations permit
Drip irrigation combined with soil moisture monitoring, concentrating water application at critical periods (around véraison).
📋 Operating Principles
  • Avoid frequent light watering → shallow roots
  • Infrequent but sufficient → encourages deep roots
  • Withhold water after véraison → concentrate flavours
🎯 Goal: "Moderate water stress" rather than high-yield irrigation
🚜
Reducing Compaction and Erosion
Protecting soil pore structure
Rotate machinery routes sensibly, reduce machine traffic on wet soil; use contour farming and grass strips on slopes.
⚠️ Compaction Hazards
  • Porosity ↓ → reduced permeability
  • Shallow root formation
  • Increased risk of anaerobic conditions
📊 Long-term monitoring: soil penetration resistance + infiltration rate
slides.26.title: Case Study: Precision Management in Pessac-Léognan
slides.26.content:
🏰
Château Smith Haut Lafitte
Graves / Pessac-Léognan　renowned for both red and white
Core challenge
Maintaining balance and clarity of red/white wines in extreme vintages
🌡️
Surface and Microclimate Management
🔧 Measures
  • Inter-row cover crops: increase soil carbon, stabilise moisture and cool the site
  • Biochar: improve water holding and CEC (localised)
  • Infrared thermal imaging: locate hot spots and water-deficit areas
✅ Spatial temperature/moisture variation reduced; ripening more uniform
🏗️
Structure and Compaction Management
🔧 Measures
  • Fixed machinery lanes: concentrate compaction to fewer paths
  • Deep-rooting cover crops: 'biological biopores' to loosen compacted layers
  • Delay entry after rain: avoid compacting wet soil
✅ Porosity ↑, permeability improved, deeper root penetration
🏆 Overall Outcomes
🍷 Softer tannins in heatwave years; better acidity retention in whites
⚙️ Reduced irrigation dependency; more flexible operating windows

slides.29.title: Contrast One: Gravel vs Clay
slides.29.content:
Typical sensory profiles of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
🪨
Gravel
Cabernet Sauvignon
👄 Palate Firm structure, precise lines
👃 Aromas Blackcurrant, pencil shavings, cedar, graphite
⚖️ Acid/Tannin Medium-high acidity, ripe and refined tannins
🕰️ Ageing Long (15–30 years)
Elegant restraint · Power and precision in equal measure
🧱
Clay
Merlot
👄 Palate Full body, rounded texture
👃 Aromas Plum, blackberry, truffle, iron ore
⚖️ Acid/Tannin Medium acidity, soft tannins
🕰️ Ageing Medium to long (10–20 years)
Full and deep · Approachable and generous
💡 Both can achieve high quality, but express different dimensions: gravel emphasises 'line and precision', clay emphasises 'texture and envelopment'
slides.30.title: Contrast Two: Limestone vs Sand
slides.30.content:
Different sensory dimensions of Cabernet Franc / Merlot
⛰️
Limestone
Cabernet Franc · Merlot
👄 Palate Defined backbone, fresh finish
👃 Aromas Chalk, wet stone, violet, red fruits
⚖️ Acid/Tannin High acidity, refined tannins
🕰️ Ageing Medium to long (12–25 years)
Elegant and reserved · Prominent minerality
🏖️
Sand
Early-ripening varieties
👄 Palate Light and soft, easy drinking
👃 Aromas Strawberry, cherry, floral
⚖️ Acid/Tannin Medium-high acidity, low to medium tannins

Fragrant and bright · Highly approachable

slides.31.title: Knowledge Check: Sensory Perception and Terroir Expression
slides.32.title: Soil Strategies under Climate Change
slides.32.subtitle: Resilience, Carbon, and Long-term Stability
slides.33.title: Responding to Drought and Extreme Heat
slides.33.content:
💧
Improving Soil Water Retention and Shading
Short- to medium-term response
Use cover crops and mulch to increase organic matter and water retention, and use canopy management to reduce peak heat at the cluster zone.
🔑 Core Approaches
  • Deep-rooting cover crops → biological biopores
  • Promote rapid rainfall infiltration
  • Reduce surface runoff
🌡️ In heatwave years: fruit temperature management is key to preserving acidity
🌱
Rootstock and Parcel Strategy
Long-term strategy on a decade timescale
Select drought-tolerant, deep-rooting rootstocks and place early-ripening varieties on cooler, water-retentive parcels.
🔑 Core Approaches
  • Rotation + low disturbance → increase organic carbon
  • Build 'sponge-like' soil structure
  • Reassess variety/clone selection and blending
📅 Parcel redesign is a decade-scale strategic investment
slides.34.title: Regenerative Agriculture and Soil Carbon
slides.34.content:
🌿
Low-disturbance / Permanent Cover
Core of Regenerative practice
Reduce tillage and bare-soil periods, maintaining mycorrhizal continuity to enhance carbon sequestration and resilience.
🔑 Practice Combination
  • Reduce tillage → mycorrhizal continuity ↑
  • Compost + organic amendments + biochar
  • Stabilise organic carbon pool, improve CEC
Soil carbon ↑ = stable structure + better water retention + slow-release nutrients
📊
Data-Driven Precision Management
Core of Precision farming
Build models using electrical conductivity, moisture, thermal imaging, and elevation layers for zone-based management and variable-rate application.
🔑 Practice Combination
  • EC/moisture/thermal/elevation modelling
  • Zone management + variable-rate application
  • Iterate on small parcels to reduce trial-and-error risk
Precision: complex soil → manageable multi-zone system
slides.35.title: Multi-Estate Comparison: Future-Facing Soil Strategies
slides.35.content:
Different philosophical pathways
🌿 Estate A
Regenerative Farming
🔑 Core Measures
  • Year-round cover with diverse mixed sowing
  • Low-disturbance tillage
  • High proportion of organic amendments
Long-term carbon and structure as core, fundamentally enhancing resilience
📊 Estate B
Precision Management
🔑 Core Measures
  • Zone sensing and map-based decision making
  • Variable-rate irrigation / fertilisation
  • Remote thermal imaging monitoring
Use data to shorten trial-and-error costs; precisely match resources and risks
⚖️ Estate C
Hybrid Strategy
🔑 Core Measures
  • Regenerative + precision integration
  • Parcel reconfiguration and rootstock renewal
  • Climate scenario planning exercises
Balancing long-term resilience with short-term efficiency
💡 There is no single 'correct' answer; the key is understanding your own soil and style goals, and continuously iterating

slides.38.summary: You have systematically studied the core theory of soil science, the detailed characteristics of Bordeaux's five major soil types, and the scientific mechanisms by which soil influences wine. This knowledge will help you develop a deeper understanding of the true essence of terroir, and interpret wine style and quality from a soil perspective.
